NovaBio Therapeutics - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the NovaBio Therapeutics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during this time, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss NovaBio Therapeutics' financial results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Dr. Alex Rivera, Chief Executive Officer; Jennifer Lee, Chief Financial Officer; Dr. David Kim, Chief Medical Officer; and Dr. Laura Chen, Chief Scientific Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's call will contain forward-looking statements. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Dr. Alex Rivera, CEO of NovaBio Therapeutics.

Dr. Alex Rivera, CEO:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. NovaBio Therapeutics delivered a strong performance in the third quarter, driven by robust commercial execution across our oncology and immunology franchises, alongside meaningful contributions from our rare disease portfolio and accelerating pipeline momentum. We continue to make significant progress on our key strategic priorities, including advancing our oncology-focused pipeline with assets like our lead ADC, NBX-401, and our next-generation CAR-T platform, NBX-520, while layering in value through targeted business development.

We are particularly excited about NBX-401 and its potential to transform outcomes in relapsed/refractory HER2-positive solid tumors following its recent accelerated FDA approval, with early launch indicators pointing to rapid market penetration similar to leading ADCs.

Now, I will turn the call over to Jennifer Lee, our CFO, to provide a more detailed review of our financial results.

Jennifer Lee, CFO:
Thank you, Dr. Rivera. As Dr. Rivera mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Revenue for the quarter was $2,850 million, an increase of 18% compared to the same period last year. This increase was primarily driven by strong demand for our core products in oncology and immunology, volume growth from label expansions, and partnership milestones.

Our GAAP net income for the quarter was $800 million, or $1.85 per share. Non-GAAP net income was $950 million, or $2.14 per share.

Our operating expenses were $1,083 million, reflecting disciplined investments in R&D to support our pipeline amid manufacturing efficiencies. We continue to invest heavily in R&D to fuel our late-stage assets. Our cash position remains strong at $8,700 million.

For the full year, we are updating our guidance to revenue of $11.4 to $11.6 billion and adjusted EPS of $8.40 to $8.60.

I'm pleased to share that we delivered another quarter of robust execution against our strategic priorities, posting record net revenues of $2.85 billion, up 18% year-over-year and 5% above the high end of our guidance range. This marks our ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, driven by strong demand across our core franchises in oncology, immunology, and rare diseases, as well as meaningful contributions from our recent launches and pipeline momentum.

Let me break this down by key drivers. Starting with our blockbuster portfolio: NBX-101, our next-generation PD-1/PD-L1 bispecific antibody, generated net product sales of $1.32 billion, a 22% increase year-over-year, outpacing the broader checkpoint inhibitor market. Volume growth of 14% was fueled by expanded label indications in frontline metastatic NSCLC and melanoma, where we've captured share from incumbents like Merck's Keytruda and Bristol Myers Squibb's Opdivo, thanks to our differentiated bispecific mechanism showing a 28% improvement in objective response rate in head-to-head Phase III data. In immunology, NBX-45, our IL-23 inhibitor for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and Crohn's disease, ramped to $685 million in sales—up 45% year-over-year and ahead of our internal models—benefiting from the post-Humira patent cliff dynamics, where we've secured preferred formulary positioning with major pharmacy benefit managers like CVS Caremark and Express Scripts.

Our rare disease and gene therapy segment also shone, contributing $420 million, a 32% year-over-year surge led by NBX-7, our AAV-based gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, which saw U.S. peak sales tracking toward $1.2 billion annually following FDA approval of our expanded pediatric label. Ex-U.S., partnerships with Roche and Takeda enabled first-half launches in Europe and Japan, adding $150 million in milestone and royalty revenues.

Financially, we expanded adjusted gross margins to 87.2%, up 210 basis points year-over-year, reflecting manufacturing efficiencies at our Singapore biologics facility and reduced cost of goods sold from our continuous manufacturing platform for NBX-101. Adjusted R&D expenses came in at 22% of revenues, or $627 million, supporting a record 14 Phase III readouts this year and investments in our AI-accelerated discovery engine—powered by a collaboration with NVIDIA—which has cut hit-to-lead timelines by 40% in our oncology small-molecule programs. Operating expenses were disciplined at 38% of revenues, yielding adjusted EBITDA of $1.12 billion, or 39% margins, and non-GAAP EPS of $2.14—beating consensus by $0.19. Free cash flow generation was stellar at $950 million, bolstering our balance sheet to $8.7 billion in cash and equivalents, with net debt to EBITDA at a healthy 1.2x.

Regionally, the U.S. remained our growth engine, accounting for 62% of revenues at $1.77 billion, up 21% year-over-year, propelled by Inflation Reduction Act pricing negotiations favoring our innovative profiles—NBX-101's maximum unit price cap was set 12% below peers. Europe delivered 14% growth to $720 million, with NBX-45 gaining traction amid the EMA's push for biosimilars, though we navigated headwinds from Germany's AMNOG pricing reforms. In Asia-Pacific, revenues hit $280 million, up 25%, driven by our joint venture with CSPC Pharma in China for NBX-101 biosimilars and a new licensing deal for NBX-7 with Chugai. Emerging markets grew 30% to $80 million, highlighting our focus on accessible therapies like our oral JAK inhibitor for lupus, now launched in 15 Latin American countries.

Strategically, we're leaning into three pillars: precision oncology, where our companion diagnostics for NBX-101 have achieved 92% next-generation sequencing adoption in academic centers; next-gen modalities, including three CRISPR-based candidates entering the clinic; and operational resilience, with $500 million in synergies realized from last year's $4.2 billion acquisition of a key viral vector player, enhancing our capacity amid surging demand similar to the Novartis-AveXis model. We've also advanced our ESG commitments, reducing Scope 1 emissions 25% via green chemistry at our Devens site.

Challenges persist—biosimilar erosion on our legacy TNF portfolio shaved 3 points off growth, and raw material inflation from heparin supply constraints added 50 basis points to cost of goods sold—but our 75% gross margin on new molecular entities insulates us. Macro tailwinds like the GLP-1 obesity wave indirectly boost our combo therapies, with early data from our NBX-101/semaglutide trial showing 15% enhanced progression-free survival in obese NSCLC patients.

Key takeaways: One, our diversified portfolio and pipeline—28 late-stage assets, including five potential blockbusters by 2027—position us for sustained 15-18% compound annual growth rate through the decade. Two, we're raising full-year 2024 revenue guidance to $11.4-11.6 billion from $11.2-11.5 billion and adjusted EPS to $8.40-8.60 from $8.20-8.40, implying 12% EPS growth. Three, with a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 14x versus peers at 18x, we're undervalued on our innovation flywheel. We're executing at high velocity in a biotech landscape ripe for consolidators—stay tuned for Q4 updates on our BTK degrader IND and potential M&A.

As we dive deeper into our operating expense analysis, total GAAP operating expenses for the quarter came in at approximately $1.083 billion, up 18% year-over-year but flat quarter-over-quarter. On a non-GAAP basis, excluding about $12 million in one-time restructuring charges related to site optimization in Cambridge, Massachusetts, operating expenses were around $1.071 billion, representing roughly 38% of our total revenue of $2.85 billion. This keeps us on track with our full-year guidance of $4.4 to $4.6 billion in total operating expenses, implying a non-GAAP operating expense-to-revenue ratio of around 36-38%.

Breaking it down by major categories, our largest bucket was research and development, which accounted for $627 million, or about 58% of total operating expenses—up around 22% year-over-year. This increase was primarily driven by ramped-up investments in our late-stage pipeline, particularly the Phase 3 ENCORE trial for NBX-300, our next-gen PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody in oncology, which is enrolling over 1,200 patients across 150 sites globally. We accrued roughly $200 million in external clinical costs here, including contract research organization fees to players like IQVIA and PPD, up 35% year-over-year due to accelerated timelines aiming for a BLA submission to the FDA by mid-2025. Manufacturing scale-up for our bispecific platform also contributed substantially, as we validated our continuous manufacturing process at our new facility in Singapore to support commercial launch.

That said, we're already seeing early efficiencies from our AI-driven drug discovery platform, NovaBio AI Nexus, which leverages generative models similar to those from Insilico Medicine or Exscientia. In the quarter, this reduced our small-molecule hit-to-lead cycle by 40%, shaving several million off preclinical expenses compared to our internal benchmarks. Headcount in R&D grew modestly by 5% year-over-year to around 1,850 full-time equivalents, focused on our gene therapy programs in rare diseases, including our AAV-based candidate for Duchenne muscular dystrophy partnering with Sarepta Therapeutics.

Shifting to selling, general, and administrative expenses at roughly $350 million—up 9% year-over-year but down 2% sequentially—this category represented about 32% of operating expenses and was propelled by our U.S. commercial launch of NBX-Ob1, our GLP-1/GIP dual agonist for obesity, which is gaining traction post its Q1 FDA approval amid the booming market led by Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy. We expanded our specialty sales force by 15% to 450 representatives, incurring elevated compensation and promotional speaker programs. Marketing spend included significant direct-to-consumer digital campaigns targeting the 100 million U.S. adults with obesity.

Regionally, U.S. SG&A dominated at 65% of the total, reflecting our multibillion peak sales potential for NBX-Ob1 in the domestic market. Europe contributed 20%, with incremental costs for EMA reimbursement negotiations in Germany and France, where pricing pressures from the G-BA have capped our average selling price at €850 per dose versus $1,200 in the U.S. Asia-Pacific was 15%, buoyed by our J&J ex-China license deal for NBX-300, which triggered a milestone payment in the quarter—expensed as collaboration R&D but with offsetting revenue recognition.

Our other operating expenses came in lower year-over-year, thanks to facility consolidations. We completed the wind-down of our legacy sterile fill-finish operations in Switzerland, generating annual savings, and shifted to a hybrid model with Lonza for biosimilar production.

Strategically, these investments are yielding a strong return on investment. Our R&D efficiency ratio—measuring pipeline value created per dollar spent—improved to 4.2x from 3.8x last year, driven by a 25% increase in our net present value from pipeline advancements, per our internal discounted cash flow models. We're mitigating cost inflation through targeted initiatives: 20% of our discovery work is now outsourced to low-cost contract research organizations in India via Syngene, reducing full-time equivalent costs by 15%; we've implemented zero-based budgeting for general and administrative, trimming travel and IT by 8%; and our ESG-linked supply chain program with suppliers like Catalent ensures 10-12% raw material cost savings amid active pharmaceutical ingredient shortages.

Looking forward, we expect R&D to moderate slightly as ENCORE enrollment peaks, with SG&A stabilizing post-NBX-Ob1 launch ramp. Full-year non-GAAP operating expense growth will be 15-17% year-over-year, below revenue growth of 25-30%, expanding our operating margins to 28-30%. This positions us competitively against peers like Regeneron and Gilead, who are facing similar R&D inflation from immuno-oncology and cell therapy escalations.

Before I discuss our outlook, I'd like to update you on our business development activities—specifically licensing deals, acquisitions, and partnerships—which continue to be a cornerstone of our strategy to build a robust, diversified pipeline in high-growth areas like immuno-oncology, gene editing, and antibody-drug conjugates. In a market where large pharmas are facing patent cliffs on blockbusters like Keytruda and Stelara—projected to lose over $20 billion in peak sales by 2028—we've been aggressive in layering in late-stage assets and bolt-on capabilities to sustain our mid-teens revenue compound annual growth rate through 2030.

On licensing deals, we've closed three transformative in-licenses this quarter alone, adding over $1.8 billion in potential milestone value. First, we in-licensed global rights—ex-China—to Phase III-ready bispecific T-cell engager BST-301 from SynthoBio AG, a German precision oncology specialist. This asset targets solid tumors in non-small cell lung cancer with a differentiated HER2/HER3 binding profile that showed a 42% objective response rate in the ongoing pivotal trial readout last month, outperforming benchmarks from Roche's Columvi. We paid $250 million upfront, with up to $1.2 billion in biobucks tied to regulatory and sales milestones, plus tiered royalties starting at 18% on net sales above $500 million. This deal fills a gap in our immuno-oncology portfolio and positions us to capture a slice of the $50 billion global NSCLC market, growing at 12% compound annual growth rate amid rising EGFR-mutant prevalence.

Second, out-licensing remains a key monetization tool for our earlier-stage assets. We out-licensed our next-gen mRNA-LNP platform for rare liver diseases to Japan's Takeda for $150 million upfront and $800 million in milestones. Early data from our IND-enabling studies demonstrated 75% higher hepatic transfection efficiency versus Moderna's legacy tech, addressing a critical need in the $15 billion alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and Wilson's disease space. Royalties here are mid-teens, with Takeda handling all ex-U.S. development—allowing us to derisk while retaining U.S. rights and manufacturing know-how.

Third, a tuck-in license from a stealth CRISPR startup for our allogeneic CAR-T program in hematologic malignancies: $75 million upfront for ex-U.S. rights to CTX-450, which hit 65% complete response rates in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Phase I/IIa. This bolsters our cell therapy footprint amid the post-Yescarta/Kymriah consolidation wave.

Turning to acquisitions, we've executed two strategic buys totaling $2.4 billion, delivering immediate pipeline accretion and cost synergies. The headline is our $1.8 billion acquisition of AuraGenix Biotech, a U.S.-based ADC pioneer with a Phase II HER2-ADC, ARG-102, enrolling 400 patients across breast and gastric cancers. Topline data expected Q2 2025 showed a 35% progression-free survival improvement over Enhertu in interim analysis, with a cleaner safety profile—no grade 4 interstitial lung disease signals that have plagued competitors. We financed this with $900 million cash, $600 million in stock, and $300 million deferred, projecting $120 million in annual R&D synergies by consolidating our linker-payload tech stacks. AuraGenix brings three preclinical ADCs targeting underserved targets like NECTIN-4, aligning with the ADC market's explosive 25% compound annual growth rate to $30 billion by 2028.

Complementing this, we snapped up UK-based NeuroVance for $600 million all-cash, gaining their AAV9 gene therapy platform for SMA and DMD—Phase I/II data mirrors Novartis' Zolgensma but with 40% lower vector dosing via proprietary capsid engineering. This shores up our neuromuscular franchise, where we're seeing tailwinds from expanded newborn screening programs in Europe.

On partnerships, our alliances are firing on all cylinders, contributing $220 million in Q3 milestone receipts and option exercises—up 35% year-over-year. We've expanded our global co-development pact with Pfizer on our PROTAC degrader platform, now covering three additional oncology targets after positive Phase I pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics data. Pfizer funds 70% of costs, with us retaining 50/50 profit split ex-China; this mirrors the AbbVie-Celgene model that de-risked BTK degraders.

Regionally, we're doubling down on Asia-Pacific to tap into that market's 11% growth versus 5% in the U.S./EU. A new strategic alliance with China's Innovent Biologics licenses our PD-1/VEGF bispecific for Greater China rights—$100 million upfront, $650 million milestones—leveraging their Tyvyt commercial infrastructure, which generated $2.5 billion in 2023 sales. Meanwhile, in Japan, our tie-up with Astellas on a radiopharma radioligand therapy for PSMA-positive prostate cancer advanced to IND filing, with shared Phase II costs and royalties in the low 20s.

Strategically, these moves reflect our "acquire, in-license, partner" playbook: 60% of our top-10 pipeline assets now stem from business development, reducing internal discovery burn from 28% of operating expenses in 2022 to 19% today. We've achieved 15% pipeline productivity uplift via integrated AI-driven target identification from our AuraGenix acquisition, screening 5,000+ modalities quarterly. Risks include integration delays and milestone timing, but our $3.2 billion cash runway—post these deals—gives us dry powder for more, targeting two to three additional transactions in 2025 focused on cardiometabolics to counter GLP-1 dominance from Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Novo Nordisk's Ozempic.

In summary, business development has supercharged our net present value to $18 billion, up 22% quarter-over-quarter, positioning NovaBio as a top-quartile mid-cap biotech.

Thank you, Jennifer. Before I hand it over to Dr. Kim, let me quickly touch on our outlook. Our forward-looking statements are subject to the risks and uncertainties outlined in our SEC filings, including our most recent 10-Q and 10-K. These statements are made under the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Actual results could differ materially due to a variety of factors, which I'll outline explicitly.

As we guide to FY 2025 revenues of $13.2 to $14.0 billion—representing 18-25% year-over-year growth at the midpoint—our projections are anchored in several core assumptions rooted in our oncology-focused pipeline, particularly our lead ADC asset, NBX-401, and our next-gen CAR-T platform, NBX-520. Let me break these down systematically.

First, commercial execution for NBX-401. We're assuming a U.S. launch ramp-up post our recent accelerated FDA approval for relapsed/refractory HER2-positive solid tumors, with Q4 2024 peak quarterly sales stabilizing at $450 million by mid-2026. This factors in a 75% market penetration in the second-line setting within 18 months, mirroring Enhertu's trajectory from Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca, which captured 65% share in a similar indication within two years. Pricing is assumed at a wholesale acquisition cost of $185,000 per treatment course, with net pricing holding at 82% of wholesale acquisition cost after rebates—conservative given ongoing 340B negotiations but supported by our patient assistance programs capping out-of-pocket at $5 per infusion.

Regionally, we project 60% of NBX-401 sales from the U.S., 25% from Europe post-EMA approval expected Q2 2025, and 15% from Asia-Pacific, including a J-code in Japan by year-end via our partnership with Takeda. EU uptake assumes successful health technology assessment negotiations in Germany and France, with average selling prices at €140,000—10% below U.S. levels, in line with recent ICER reviews on ADCs.

Second, pipeline milestones. For NBX-520, our autologous CAR-T targeting BCMA in multiple myeloma, we assume 90% patient enrollment completion in our pivotal Phase 3 PIVOT-3 trial by Q3 2025, with topline data in Q1 2026. This implies a 25% overall response rate and 12-month progression-free survival, benchmarked against Bristol Myers Squibb's Abecma 23% overall response rate in KarMMa and Janssen's Carvykti 98% overall response rate but with higher cytokine release syndrome rates. Biologics license application submission follows in H1 2026, with approval odds at 70% based on our internal Bayesian modeling—above the industry Phase 3 success rate of 55% for cell therapies per BIO's 2023 report.

We're also baking in $500 million in milestone payments from our Regeneron collaboration on bispecific antibodies, triggered by Phase 2 readouts in Q4 2025. Manufacturing assumptions include a 20% yield improvement from our viral vector scale-up at our North Carolina facility, reducing cost of goods sold to 18% of sales for NBX-520—critical as vector supply constraints have plagued peers like bluebird bio.

Broader portfolio: Legacy small-molecule revenue from our PARP inhibitor NBX-210 grows 5% to $800 million, offset by generic erosion post-patent expiry in 2027, but bolstered by label expansions into ovarian cancer combos with Keytruda. Overall R&D spend holds at 28% of revenue, or $900 million, assuming 15% cost efficiencies from AI-driven target identification via our Insilico Medicine partnership, cutting preclinical timelines by 30%.

Macro assumptions: U.S. pharmacy benefit manager rebates stabilize at 45% versus 50% peak in 2023, inflation at 2.5%, and biologics inflation rebate caps under the Inflation Reduction Act limiting exposure to $150 million annually. We project 12% EPS growth to $9.50-$10.00, with free cash flow of $2.5 billion supporting $1 billion in buybacks.

While our assumptions are grounded in robust data, several risks could materially impact outcomes. I'll categorize them for clarity.

Pipeline and clinical risks remain the primary driver of volatility: Biotech's binary nature means clinical failures are our top risk. NBX-401's post-approval confirmatory trial carries a 15% risk of futility based on interim data monitoring committee reviews—similar to the 12% Phase 3 failure rate for ADCs in 2024 per Evaluate Pharma. For NBX-520, cytokine release syndrome/neurotoxicity risks could delay enrollment by 6 months, as seen with Legend Biotech's CAR-T halts. Overall pipeline success probability is 45% from Phase 2 onward, per our Monte Carlo simulations, below the 50% industry average due to our high-bar immuno-oncology focus. Any adverse events could trigger FDA clinical holds, eroding $1.5 billion in projected peak sales.

Regulatory and reimbursement risks: FDA/EMA timelines could slip 3-6 months amid staffing shortages—evident in Pfizer's recent Seagen integration delays. In Europe, negative innovative medicines scientific committee reviews, like Novartis' Pluvicto in 2024, could haircut EU sales by 40%. U.S. pricing reforms under Medicare Part D redesign pose a $200 million headwind if average selling price caps extend to commercial plans, exacerbated by IRA negotiations selecting our PARP for 2027 price controls 9% annual reduction risk.

Manufacturing and supply chain risks: Dependence on CDMOs like Lonza for 40% of our ADC payloads exposes us to shortages—recall the 2023 heparin crisis impacting 15% of U.S. injectables. A 10% yield shortfall in our Singapore plasmid facility could inflate NBX-520 cost of goods sold to 35%, wiping out $300 million in margins. Geopolitical tensions in Taiwan 90% of global CDMO capacity add a 5% supply disruption probability.

Competitive and IP risks: Intensifying ADC competition from Roche's Polivy combos and Merck's next-gen candidates could cap NBX-401 share at 50% versus our 75% base case, per IQVIA TRx data. Patent challenges from generics on NBX-210 Paragraph IV litigation pending risk accelerated erosion, potentially $400 million revenue loss by 2028—mirroring Eli Lilly's Alimta cliff.

Macro and market risks: Recessionary pressures could slow trial site activation by 20%, as in 2023's NIH budget cuts. Funding environment for biotechs tightens with 10-year Treasury yields above 4%, raising our $2 billion debt cost by 50 basis points. China market entry via our WuXi AppTec JV assumes 15% compound annual growth rate but faces CFDA delays amid U.S.-China trade frictions.

Strategic mitigants: To de-risk, we're advancing 10 Phase 2 assets for pipeline diversity, pursuing bolt-on M&A such as a $750 million tuck-in for rare disease gene therapy, and hedging 60% of raw material costs. Our $8.7 billion cash position provides 24 months runway at current burn.

In summary, our FY 2025 guidance embeds prudent assumptions with clear upsides from execution, but investors should weigh these risks—quantified in our investor deck's sensitivity analysis showing a 25% revenue swing on binary outcomes.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Dr. David Kim, our Chief Medical Officer, to discuss our clinical programs.

Dr. David Kim, Chief Medical Officer:
Thank you, Jennifer. We are very pleased with the progress of our clinical trials, particularly a series of high-impact regulatory approvals and label expansions that position us for multi-billion-dollar revenue inflection points over the next 24 to 36 months.

Let me start with our crown jewel, NBX-401, our next-generation antibody-drug conjugate targeting HER2-low metastatic breast cancer. In late September, the FDA granted full accelerated approval for NBX-401 as a second-line therapy post-trastuzumab deruxtecan, based on our pivotal Phase 3 AURORA trial, which demonstrated a 42% objective response rate and a median progression-free survival of 11.2 months versus 5.8 months for physician's choice chemotherapy—a hazard ratio of 0.52 that beat our statistical assumptions handily. This approval came in 2 months ahead of the PDUFA target date, thanks to our Breakthrough Therapy Designation and alignment with the FDA's Oncology Center of Excellence priorities on real-world evidence integration from our expanded access program.

The label includes our novel companion diagnostic, the NovaBio HER2-Low NGS assay, which we've co-developed with Illumina—enabling precision patient selection with 95% concordance to immunohistochemistry/in situ hybridization standards. We're projecting peak U.S. sales for NBX-401 to exceed $1.2 billion annually by 2028, capturing 18-22% share in the $7 billion HER2-low metastatic breast cancer market, currently dominated by Enhertu and Trodelvy. Incremental Q4 revenue from U.S. launch is already tracking at $45 million, with uptake 30% ahead of our internal models due to strong key opinion leader advocacy at ESMO 2024.

Building on this, we've secured two critical label expansions for our blockbuster immunology franchise, NBX-45, our IL-23 inhibitor akin to Tremfya but with a best-in-class subcutaneous every-six-months dosing profile. First, the FDA approved expansion to moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa in adults, supported by our Phase 3 HIDRA-2 study showing 58% HiSCR50 response at week 16—15 points superior to secukinumab head-to-head data. This taps a $2.5 billion U.S. opportunity where adalimumab holds 60% share but faces biosimilar erosion post-patent expiry next year.

Second, the EMA granted a positive CHMP opinion—with formal approval expected Q1 2025—for pediatric use in plaque psoriasis ages 6+, based on extrapolation from adult pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics modeling and our pediatric investigator-initiated trial. This expands our EU label six months ahead of schedule, addressing a key risk evaluation and mitigation strategy gap and unlocking €300 million in additional EU revenue by 2027. Regionally, U.S. NBX-45 sales grew 28% year-over-year to $312 million in Q3, while ex-U.S.—led by Japan PMDA approval in hidradenitis suppurativa last quarter—surged 45%, now representing 22% of franchise total. We're on track for $1.8 billion full-year NBX-45 revenue, with label expansions adding $400 million in 2025 upside.

Beyond oncology and immunology, we achieved orphan drug designation and NMPA approval in China for NBX-7R, our CRISPR/Cas9-based ex vivo gene therapy for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia. This follows our U.S. regenerative medicine advanced therapy designation and builds on positive 24-month data from the BEACON trial: 92% transfusion independence rate in the high-fetal hemoglobin cohort. Partnering with Fosun Pharma, we're launching in Tier-1 cities Q2 2025, targeting a $1 billion China market amid the NMPA's push for cell/gene therapies—we've already secured reimbursement in Shanghai at ¥1.2 million per dose, competitive with Zynteglo.

Strategically, these wins reflect our 'label-first, lifecycle-max' approach: 70% of our 2024 regulatory submissions leveraged real-world evidence from our global patient registry—now 25,000+ strong—cutting Phase 3 timelines by 18 months on average. We've filed four additional supplemental new drug applications/supplemental biologics license applications this quarter, including NBX-401 frontline expansion and NBX-45 in Crohn's maintenance, with PDUFA dates clustered in H1 2025. This de-risks our $15 billion peak sales pipeline potential across 10+ labels by 2030.

From a valuation lens, these catalysts justify our forward price-to-sales multiple expansion to 8.5x—in line with Regeneron post-Dupixent expansions—and support our raised 2025 guidance of $13.2-14.0 billion total revenue, up 22% at midpoint. Ex-U.S. now 35% of mix, up from 28% last year, mitigating U.S. pricing headwinds under the Inflation Reduction Act.

We expect to achieve several upcoming milestones, including topline data from PIVOT-3 and additional label expansions.

Now, I'll hand the call back to Dr. Rivera.

Dr. Alex Rivera, CEO:
Thank you, Dr. Kim. We will now open the call for questions.

Operator:
[Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith, Goldman Sachs:
Thanks for taking my question. Jennifer, could you elaborate on the key assumptions behind the NBX-401 launch ramp and any competitive risks you're seeing in the ADC space?

Jennifer Lee, CFO:
Thanks, John. Great question. As I detailed earlier, our NBX-401 assumptions are conservative, projecting 75% market penetration in the second-line HER2-positive setting within 18 months, based on Enhertu's real-world trajectory. Peak quarterly sales of $450 million by mid-2026 factor in U.S. wholesale acquisition cost pricing at $185,000 per course, with 82% net realization post-rebates. Competitively, we're monitoring Roche and Merck entrants, but our cleaner safety profile and companion diagnostic give us an edge—our Monte Carlo models cap share loss at 25% downside. Sensitivity analysis in our deck shows resilience even if penetration hits 50%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Gonzalez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Maria Gonzalez, JPMorgan:
Hi, team. David, on the label expansions for NBX-45, how do you see the hidradenitis suppurativa uptake playing out, especially with biosimilar pressures?

Dr. David Kim, Chief Medical Officer:
Thanks, Maria. The HS expansion is a game-changer, tapping a $2.5 billion market with our 58% HiSCR50 from HIDRA-2 outperforming secukinumab. Biosimilars erode adalimumab, but our Q6M dosing drives differentiation—early U.S. scripts are 30% above model, and Japan PMDA win accelerates ex-U.S. to 22% of sales. Pediatric psoriasis in EU adds €300 million by 2027, with four more filings in H1 2025.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Patel, Morgan Stanley:
Thanks. Jennifer, any color on operating expense trajectory into 2025, given the BD deals and R&D ramp?

Jennifer Lee, CFO:
Absolutely, David. Q4 operating expenses will trend toward $1.05-1.1 billion non-GAAP as ENCORE peaks, with full-year growth at 15-17% below revenue. Efficiencies from AI Nexus and Syngene outsourcing keep R&D at 22-28% of sales, while AuraGenix synergies deliver $120 million annually. Our 4.2x R&D efficiency ratio supports margin expansion to 28-30%, even with pipeline investments.

Operator:
[No further questions at this time.]

Dr. Alex Rivera, CEO:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I want to thank our employees for their hard work and dedication. We are confident in our ability to continue to execute on our strategic priorities and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.
